goldens.comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.

The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.

The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.

uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.
Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.

adjudication_records.issue_text: renderEmail is called with template names 'AttendeeAddGuestsEmail' and 'OrganizerAddGuestsEmail' that have no case in renderEmail's dispatch mapping, so add-guests emails render as wrong/default template or throw at render time, with errors swallowed in catch and success falsely reported

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows new template classes calling `renderEmail("AttendeeAddGuestsEmail", ...)` and `renderEmail("OrganizerAddGuestsEmail", ...)`, but it does not include `renderEmail`’s implementation/dispatch table, so we cannot verify the claim that these names are missing and would render the wrong/default template or throw. While `addGuests.handler.ts` does catch and swallow errors from `sendAddGuestsEmails`, the specific root cause asserted (missing renderEmail mapping for those template names) is not provable from the provided diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: New template entries in src/templates/index.ts are named exports that nothing imports, while email-manager imports parallel class-based default exports — two hand-wired template hierarchies with only one of each used (advisory)

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows two layers that appear intentionally parallel: (1) class-based email sender templates in `packages/emails/templates/*.ts` that `email-manager.ts` imports and uses to build nodemailer payloads, and (2) React render templates in `packages/emails/src/templates/*.tsx` that are referenced by `renderEmail("AttendeeAddGuestsEmail"|"OrganizerAddGuestsEmail", ...)`. The finding’s key assertion that the new `src/templates/index.ts` named exports are "imported by nothing" cannot be verified from this diff (they may be used indirectly by the render system or elsewhere), and the presence of both hierarchies does not, from the diff alone, indicate only one is used.

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts:50-52 — permission check uses && instead of ||, so team admins who are not owners are incorrectly denied (FORBIDDEN)
matched_golden_ids: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate flags the same permission-check logic error: using && instead of ||, which incorrectly requires a user to be both team admin and owner rather than either one.

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts:77-79 — blacklist comparison is case-sensitive against a lowercased list, allowing mixed-case blacklisted emails to bypass the blacklist
BookingListItem.tsx:193-199 — 'additional_guests' action is rendered unconditionally for every booking status, allowing guests to be added to cancelled/rejected/pending bookings

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds an "add_members" action to the `actions` array in `BookingListItem` without any check against `booking.status` (it’s appended unconditionally alongside other actions). On the backend, `addGuestsHandler` also does not validate booking status before mutating attendees, so cancelled/rejected/pending bookings would still be eligible for adding guests if the UI exposes the action. This makes the finding a plausible, diff-grounded correctness issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts — no tests for the new mutation (permission matrix, blacklist filter, duplicate filtering, seat fields) anywhere in the diff

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new nontrivial `viewer.bookings.addGuests` mutation and handler (`packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts`) with permission checks (`isTeamAdmin`/`isTeamOwner`/organizer/attendee), blacklist filtering via `BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS`, duplicate/existing-attendee filtering (`uniqueGuests`), and calendar/email side effects (`eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees`, `sendAddGuestsEmails`). No test files or test changes are included anywhere in the diff to validate this behavior or its edge cases, so the finding is accurate and actionable.

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts:136-138,155 — seat-based bookings (seatsPerTimeSlot) passed into evt but guests still written via attendees.createMany, ignoring the seats attendee model

adjudication.rationale: The handler always appends new guests via `prisma.booking.update({ data: { attendees: { createMany: ... }}})` and also copies `seatsPerTimeSlot`/`seatsShowAttendees` from `booking.eventType` onto the `evt` object. However, the diff does not show any separate “seats attendee model” or alternative persistence path that should be used for seat-based bookings, so the claim that it is “ignoring” that model is not verifiable from the provided changes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts:74-83 — attendee-gated authorization lets any attendee add unlimited guests; no max() cap on the guests array in the schema

adjudication.rationale: In addGuests.handler.ts the authorization explicitly allows any existing attendee to add guests (`const isAttendee = !!booking.attendees.find(...);` and then `if (!isTeamAdminOrOwner && !isOrganizer && !isAttendee) throw FORBIDDEN;`). That means any attendee on a booking can mutate the attendee list and trigger calendar updates + emails, which is a security/abuse risk if not intended. Additionally, the server-side schema `ZAddGuestsInputSchema` defines `guests: z.array(z.string().email())` with no `.max(...)` (and the UI also allows adding arbitrarily many), enabling unbounded guest additions/spam.

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts:66-68 / AddGuestsDialog.tsx:13-15 — duplicate detection is exact-case both client and server, treating a@b.com and A@b.com as distinct attendees; client schema duplicates server schema validation and can drift

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows email comparisons and filtering are case-sensitive. In `addGuests.handler.ts`, `uniqueGuests` is computed via exact string equality (`guest === attendee.email`) and blacklist checking compares lowercased blacklist entries to the raw `guest` (`blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`), so `A@b.com` can bypass both “already an attendee” and the blacklist if `a@b.com` is present/blacklisted. On the client, the dialog’s local `ZAddGuestsInputSchema` uses a `Set` over the raw strings (no lowercasing), so `a@b.com` and `A@b.com` are treated as distinct too. Additionally, the client defines its own validation schema inside `AddGuestsDialog.tsx` while the server has a separate `addGuests.schema.ts`, creating duplicated validation logic that can drift.

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts:53-55: isTeamAdminOrOwner uses && instead of ||, denying team admins (non-owners) permission and making the admin check dead code — blocking

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed as `(await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))` (lines ~53-55). Given the variable name and typical permission semantics, this should be `||`; as written it only allows users who are both admin and owner, denying team admins who aren’t owners and effectively making the “admin” branch not grant access by itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts:49-66: No booking.status check allows adding guests to cancelled/rejected bookings and sending iCal invites for dead bookings — blocking

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, the booking is fetched by `id` only (`prisma.booking.findFirst({ where: { id: bookingId } ... })`) and then updated/sends calendar/email updates with no guard on any booking state/status before creating attendees and issuing `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(...)` + `sendAddGuestsEmails(...)`. The diff does not show whether `booking.status` exists or what the intended business rule is for cancelled/rejected bookings, so it’s not strictly verifiable as a defect, but it is a concrete, diff-grounded missing edge-case validation for a potentially invalid state transition.

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts:63-66: Any booking attendee gains write access to the guest list, allowing arbitrary emails to be added that receive event details and video-call link — blocking scope expansion

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, authorization explicitly permits any existing attendee to add guests: `const isAttendee = !!booking.attendees.find((attendee) => attendee.email === user.email);` and the guard only blocks when the user is not team admin/owner, not organizer, and not attendee (`if (!isTeamAdminOrOwner && !isOrganizer && !isAttendee) throw FORBIDDEN`). The handler then appends new attendee records and builds a `CalendarEvent` including `videoCallData` (if present) and calls `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` plus `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)`, where newly-added emails receive `AttendeeScheduledEmail` (full event details/ICS). This means any attendee can add arbitrary emails and cause them to receive event details (and potentially video link), which matches the finding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts:169-172: Email send failure is swallowed with console.log (error object not even logged) and client is told success — silent delivery loss, advisory

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, the new email notification side-effect is wrapped in `try { await sendAddGuestsEmails(...) } catch (err) { console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails"); }`, which both (a) discards the actual error object and (b) continues to return success (`return { message: "Guests added" }`) even when email delivery fails. This is a concrete, diff-grounded reliability/observability issue for the newly added email feature, but not necessarily a hard correctness defect since the primary operation (adding attendees + calendar update) still succeeds.

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts:70-77: Blacklisted and duplicate guest emails are silently dropped with no feedback, and error message emails_must_be_unique_valid misdescribes the failure — advisory

adjudication.rationale: In addGuests.handler.ts the handler builds `uniqueGuests` by filtering out emails that are already in `booking.attendees` and those in `BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS` (the `guests.filter(...)` block). Any filtered-out entries are simply omitted with no response indicating which were skipped. Additionally, when all submitted guests are filtered out (`uniqueGuests.length === 0`), it throws `BAD_REQUEST` with message `emails_must_be_unique_valid`, which is misleading because the failure can be due to blacklist/existing-attendee filtering, not invalid format (input schema already enforces `.email()`). This is a concrete UX/error-message issue, not a clear functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts:81-85: No upper bound on guest count (unbounded email array) and dedupe compares raw strings without case normalization — advisory

adjudication.rationale: The new TRPC input schema `ZAddGuestsInputSchema` allows `guests: z.array(z.string().email())` with no `.max(...)`, and the handler uses it to `createMany` attendees and `Promise.all` send emails (`sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)`), so a very large array could trigger excessive DB writes/emails (resource/DoS risk). Also, deduping/duplicate checks compare raw strings (`guest === attendee.email`) without case normalization, while the blacklist is lowercased, so case-variant duplicates can slip through.

adjudication_records.issue_text: MultiEmail.tsx: Shared UI component keyed by array index, so removing an email shifts values onto wrong controlled inputs — advisory

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/ui/form/MultiEmail.tsx`, the list renders `value.map((field, index) => (<li key={index}> ...))` and removes items via `updatedValue.splice(index, 1)`. Using the array index as a React key is a real, diff-grounded concern because removing an entry changes subsequent indices, which can cause React to reuse component instances incorrectly (e.g., focus/caret/validation UI sticking to the wrong row). However, the inputs are controlled via `value={field}`, so the claim that values will definitively “shift onto wrong controlled inputs” isn’t strictly verifiable as a guaranteed defect from the diff alone; it’s more of an advisory robustness/UX issue.

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts:51 — team-admin check is ANDed with team-owner check, so only owners can add guests despite intent of admin-or-owner

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed with `&&`: `(await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))`, which requires the user to be both a team admin and a team owner. Given the variable name and typical permission intent, this logic excludes admins who are not owners, matching the finding that only owners effectively pass this check.

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts:88-93 — duplicate attendee check is case-sensitive exact-string, so same email in different casing is treated as new guest, creating duplicate rows and double emails

adjudication.rationale: In addGuests.handler.ts the duplicate check uses exact string equality (`guest === attendee.email`) when filtering `uniqueGuests`, without normalizing casing. As a result, adding `Test@Example.com` when `test@example.com` already exists will bypass the check, create a duplicate attendee via `createMany`, and trigger additional calendar/email notifications.

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts:88-93 — blacklist check compares non-lowercased guest against lowercased blacklist, so differently-cased blacklisted emails never match

adjudication.rationale: In addGuests.handler.ts, blacklistedGuestEmails are normalized to lowercase (split(...).map(email => email.toLowerCase())), but the filter uses !blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) where guest is taken directly from input without lowercasing. This means a blacklisted email like "test@example.com" will not match an input guest "Test@Example.com", allowing differently-cased blacklisted emails through.

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.schema.ts:4-7 vs AddGuestsDialog.tsx:18-21 — client and server schema copies have drifted: client has uniqueness refine, server lacks uniqueness/case normalization, no single source of truth

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows two separate Zod schemas for the same payload: AddGuestsDialog.tsx defines a local `ZAddGuestsInputSchema` with a uniqueness `refine`, while the server `addGuests.schema.ts` only validates `guests` as `z.array(z.string().email())` with no uniqueness check. Since the server handler’s `uniqueGuests` filter only removes existing attendees/blacklisted emails (not duplicates within the input), a caller can bypass the client and send duplicate emails, which can lead to duplicate attendee creates (or a DB constraint error) and inconsistent behavior. The “single source of truth”/drift concern is real and grounded in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts:97-107 — check-then-insert TOCTOU on attendees with no UNIQUE(bookingId, email) index allows duplicate attendee rows under concurrency

adjudication.rationale: In addGuests.handler.ts the code reads existing attendees (booking.attendees) to compute uniqueGuests, then later inserts via prisma.booking.update(... attendees.createMany ...). This is a classic check-then-insert pattern that is not concurrency-safe and can allow duplicate attendee rows or unexpected insert failures if two addGuests mutations run concurrently. However, the finding’s claim that there is "no UNIQUE(bookingId, email) index" cannot be verified from this diff (no schema/migration shown), so the exact impact (duplicates vs. constraint error) isn’t provable here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: addGuests.handler.ts:158-162 — calendar update uses caller's credentials instead of organizer's/booking's, so when an attendee adds guests the wrong calendar account is mutated

adjudication.rationale: In addGuests.handler.ts the calendar update is performed with credentials derived from the authenticated caller: `const credentials = await getUsersCredentials(ctx.user);` and `new EventManager({ ...user, credentials: [...credentials] })`, then `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)`. Since the handler explicitly allows non-organizers (an attendee) to call it (`isAttendee` check), an attendee adding guests will attempt to mutate the event using the attendee’s connected calendar credentials rather than the booking organizer’s (which is fetched separately as `organizer` but not used for credentials). This can update the wrong calendar account or fail to update the organizer’s calendar, matching the finding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: ADVISORY — addGuests.handler.ts:97 — no cap on guests array size; unbounded attendees materialized and emailed, and re-adds resend emails to all attendees

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `addGuests` with input schema `guests: z.array(z.string().email())` in `addGuests.schema.ts` with no `.max()`/cap, and `addGuests.handler.ts` uses that array to `createMany` attendees and then sends emails in bulk (`Promise.all`) via `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)`, which iterates over `calendarEvent.attendees` and emails every attendee. This creates a verifiable resource-exhaustion/spam vector (unbounded writes + unbounded outbound emails) introduced by the change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: ADVISORY — addGuests.handler.ts:64 — attendees can add guests to seated events with no seatsPerTimeSlot capacity enforcement

adjudication.rationale: The new `addGuestsHandler` allows any attendee (`isAttendee` check) to add new booking attendees, and it unconditionally creates new attendee records via `prisma.booking.update({ data: { attendees: { createMany: ... }}})` without checking `booking.eventType?.seatsPerTimeSlot` or current attendee count. Since the handler also carries `seatsPerTimeSlot` into the `CalendarEvent` (`evt.seatsPerTimeSlot = booking.eventType?.seatsPerTimeSlot`) but never enforces capacity, seated/limited-capacity events can be overfilled by adding guests.

adjudication_records.issue_text: ADVISORY — addGuests.handler.ts:170 — email failures silently console.log-logged after booking mutated, with no queue/outbox or returned warning for notification failure

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, the booking is updated and calendar attendees are updated before attempting to send notification emails. The email send is wrapped in a `try/catch` that only `console.log`s on failure (`try { await sendAddGuestsEmails(...) } catch { console.log(...) }`), and the handler still returns success (`return { message: "Guests added" }`). This creates a reliability/observability gap (no propagation/queue/outbox/retry or warning to caller) even though the core mutation succeeds.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Permission check uses `&&` instead of `||` in isTeamAdmin/isTeamOwner condition, denying team admins from adding guests (P1)

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts`, `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed with `&&` between `isTeamAdmin(...)` and `isTeamOwner(...)`, meaning the user must be both admin and owner to pass (`const isTeamAdminOrOwner = (await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...));`). This will incorrectly deny team admins (who aren’t also owners) from adding guests, contradicting the intended “admin OR owner” authorization.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Calendar mutation runs with the acting user's credentials instead of the organizer's, so organizer's calendar event is not updated with new attendees (P1)

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, the calendar update is executed via `new EventManager({ ...user, credentials: [...credentials] })` where `credentials` come from `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` (the acting user) and `user` is `ctx.user`. If a non-organizer (e.g., an attendee or team admin) adds guests—explicitly allowed by the permission checks—the mutation will attempt to update the booking’s calendar attendees using the actor’s credentials rather than the organizer’s credentials (`booking.user.credentials` is loaded but never used). This can prevent updating the organizer’s calendar event with the new attendees.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Email-sending failures swallowed with console.log, client always shows 'Guests added' success even when invites fail (P2)

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuestsHandler`, `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` is wrapped in a `try/catch` that only `console.log`s and does not rethrow (`packages/trpc/.../addGuests.handler.ts`). The mutation then still returns `{ message: "Guests added" }`, so the client `onSuccess` toast (`showToast(t("guests_added"), "success")`) will fire even if email sending fails. Whether this should be a hard failure is product-dependent, but the diff clearly makes email failures invisible to the caller and only logs them.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Parallel hand-maintained validation schemas have drifted: client enforces unique emails, server doesn't; dedup and blacklist checks are case-sensitive causing duplicate attendees and blacklist bypass (P2)

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows divergent validation: the client-side `AddGuestsDialog` defines `ZAddGuestsInputSchema = z.array(z.string().email()).refine(...)` to enforce uniqueness, but the server-side `ZAddGuestsInputSchema` in `addGuests.schema.ts` only validates `guests: z.array(z.string().email())` with no uniqueness constraint. In `addGuests.handler.ts`, both the existing-attendee check and blacklist check are case-sensitive (`guest === attendee.email` and `blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`), while the blacklist entries are lowercased but `guest` is not, enabling blacklist bypass via casing and allowing duplicate attendees differing only by case. These are verifiable correctness/security issues in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: No seat-capacity check despite seatsPerTimeSlot being read; guests can be added past seat capacity in seated bookings (P2)

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuestsHandler` the code adds new attendees via `prisma.booking.update({ data: { attendees: { createMany: ... }}})` with no validation against any seat/attendee limit (e.g., `booking.eventType?.seatsPerTimeSlot`). The handler even propagates `seatsPerTimeSlot` into the `CalendarEvent` (`evt.seatsPerTimeSlot = booking.eventType?.seatsPerTimeSlot`) but never checks whether `bookingAttendees.attendees.length + uniqueGuests.length` would exceed capacity for seated events, so guests can be added beyond the configured limit.

adjudication_records.issue_text: AddGuestsDialog sends raw multiEmailValue including empty strings, producing misleading 'Emails must be unique and valid' error, and isInvalidEmail never resets on subsequent successful validation (P3)
matched_golden_ids: Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate flags that multiEmailValue includes empty strings and that this causes misleading validation errors, which aligns with the golden concern about initializing with an empty string leading to validation issues and suggesting an empty array/empty-state handling. It also mentions an extra issue (isInvalidEmail not resetting), but the core empty-string-in-array problem matches.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Blacklist normalization mismatch: blacklistedGuestEmails is lowercased but membership check compares raw guest input, allowing case-variant emails to bypass the blacklist; must check blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest.toLowerCase()) (P1)
matched_golden_ids: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both describe the same flaw: the blacklist is lowercased but the guest email input is not, so the includes() check is case-sensitive and can be bypassed with uppercase variants. Candidate also suggests lowercasing the guest input, matching the expected fix.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Trust-the-client authorization: attendees can mutate any booking's attendee list, persist attendee rows, dispatch emails including ICS with meeting URL/password to arbitrary addresses, and mutate the organizer's calendar event; restrict mutation to organizer/team (P2)

adjudication.rationale: The new `addGuests` mutation explicitly authorizes *attendees* to add guests: `const isAttendee = !!booking.attendees.find((attendee) => attendee.email === user.email);` and then permits the mutation when `isAttendee` is true (`if (!isTeamAdminOrOwner && !isOrganizer && !isAttendee) throw ...`). Once authorized, it persists new attendee rows (`prisma.booking.update(... attendees.createMany ...)`), updates the calendar event attendees (`eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)`), and sends emails/ICS that may include video meeting data (`evt.videoCallData` from `booking.references`). This allows any existing attendee to add arbitrary external emails and trigger calendar/email distribution of meeting details, which matches the core of the finding (though not “any booking”—only bookings where the caller is an attendee).

adjudication_records.issue_text: isTeamAdminOrOwner uses && instead of ||, denying plain team admins on a flow the UI exposes (P3)

adjudication.rationale:
In `addGuests.handler.ts`, `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed with `&&`:
```ts
const isTeamAdminOrOwner = (await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...));
```
This requires the user to be both a team admin and a team owner to pass the permission check. Given the variable name and typical authorization intent (admin OR owner), this will incorrectly forbid “plain” team admins from using the newly added `addGuests` flow exposed in the UI (`BookingListItem` opens `AddGuestsDialog` and calls `viewer.bookings.addGuests`).

adjudication_records.issue_text: Case-sensitive attendee dedup: exact-match check against attendee.email lets case-variant duplicates create duplicate attendee rows; normalize emails to lowercase at input (P3)

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, dedup/filtering uses exact string comparison (`guest === attendee.email`) and the UI’s uniqueness check in `AddGuestsDialog.tsx` uses `new Set(emails)`—both are case-sensitive. Since neither the client nor server normalizes emails to lowercase, a user can add `Test@x.com` when `test@x.com` already exists, resulting in duplicate attendee rows via `attendees.createMany`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: EventManager is built from ctx.user (caller) instead of the booking's organizer, so calendar updates run with the caller's credentials against the organizer's event (P2)

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings/addGuests.handler.ts`, the calendar update is executed with the caller's identity/credentials: `const credentials = await getUsersCredentials(ctx.user);` and `new EventManager({ ...user, credentials: [...credentials] })`, where `user` comes from `ctx.user`. However the booking’s organizer is `booking.userId` and the diff even fetches `organizer` and includes `booking.user.credentials`, but those organizer credentials are not used. If the caller is an attendee or team admin/owner, this can cause `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` to run against the organizer’s booking with the wrong account credentials, leading to failed or incorrect calendar updates.

adjudication_records.issue_text: AddGuestsDialog.tsx:17-20 client-side schema is a hand-copied duplicate of the server schema ZAddGuestsInputSchema instead of importing and extending it, risking schema drift and server-side BAD_REQUEST toasts instead of inline validation

adjudication.rationale: In AddGuestsDialog.tsx the client defines its own ZAddGuestsInputSchema (an email array with a uniqueness refine) rather than reusing the server router’s ZAddGuestsInputSchema (bookingId + guests: email[]). This is a diff-grounded maintainability concern because validation rules can diverge (and already differ in shape/rules), leading to cases where the server rejects input (e.g., blacklisted/already-attendee emails) and the user only sees an error toast instead of consistent inline validation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Duplicate attendee detection is case-sensitive while the unique constraint is not: adding 'User@X.com' when 'user@x.com' exists bypasses the check, causing a P2002 500 error or duplicate attendee rows with doubled ics REQUEST emails

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, duplicate filtering compares emails case-sensitively (`guest === attendee.email`) and the client-side uniqueness check in `AddGuestsDialog` uses `new Set(emails)` which is also case-sensitive. The diff shows no normalization (e.g., `.toLowerCase()`) before checking or inserting via `createMany`, so adding `User@x.com` when `user@x.com` already exists can bypass the duplicate check and attempt to insert a logical duplicate, leading to duplicate attendee rows and/or a DB unique constraint violation if one exists.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Guest emails are not lowercased before comparison with lowercased blacklistedGuestEmails, so 'Spam@Bot.com' bypasses the blacklist and is persisted and emailed

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, `blacklistedGuestEmails` is normalized to lowercase (`.map((email) => email.toLowerCase())`), but incoming `guest` values are compared without lowercasing: `!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`. This allows case-variant emails (e.g., `Spam@Bot.com`) to bypass the blacklist and be persisted/emailed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Attendee insert is committed before updateCalendarAttendees runs with no rollback/compensation, so if the calendar update throws, DB rows permanently diverge from the external calendar event

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, the DB is updated first via `prisma.booking.update({ data: { attendees: { createMany: ... }}})` and only afterwards calls `await eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking);` with no surrounding transaction or compensation. If `updateCalendarAttendees` throws, the newly inserted attendee rows remain committed while the external calendar is not updated, causing persistent divergence between DB state and the calendar event.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Email send failure is silently swallowed with catch { console.log(...) }, so email failures are not surfaced or handled

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, email sending is wrapped in `try { await sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests); } catch (err) { console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails"); }`, which swallows the exception and only logs a generic message (no rethrow, no error propagation/telemetry). This means the mutation succeeds (`return { message: "Guests added" }`) even if notification emails fail, reducing observability and preventing callers from reacting to failures.

adjudication_records.issue_text: DB write (prisma.booking.update) committed before updateCalendarAttendees, so calendar failure returns 500 with no rollback, leaving attendees persisted but calendar unupdated and retries blocked by duplicate email validation

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, the DB is updated first via `prisma.booking.update({ data: { attendees: { createMany: ... }}})` and only afterwards the calendar is updated with `await eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking);`. There is no transaction wrapping both operations and no try/catch around `updateCalendarAttendees`, so if the calendar update throws, the mutation will fail (likely 500) while the attendees have already been persisted. A retry would then hit `uniqueGuests.length === 0` (because the emails now exist on `booking.attendees`) and throw `BAD_REQUEST`, matching the “retries blocked by duplicate email validation” part of the finding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: All email-sending failures in sendAddGuestsEmails are swallowed with only a console.log, and the handler reports 'Guests added' success even though no emails (including ICS REQUEST) were sent

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, the call to `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` is wrapped in a `try/catch` that only does `console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails")` and does not rethrow or propagate the failure. The handler then unconditionally returns `{ message: "Guests added" }`, so the mutation reports success even if all email sending (including the emails that carry the ICS REQUEST payload) fails.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Permission check uses isTeamAdmin(user.id, teamId) && isTeamOwner(user.id, teamId), requiring both roles, so non-owner team admins are always rejected with FORBIDDEN — should be || like comparable checks

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed with `(await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))`, which requires the user to be both a team admin and a team owner to pass the team-role gate. This will incorrectly reject legitimate non-owner team admins (and non-admin owners) with `FORBIDDEN` in the subsequent permission check. The variable name and typical access patterns suggest this should be `||`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: AddGuestsDialog error toast fallback is dead code because template literal is always truthy, and t(err.message) leaks raw non-locale-key error strings to the user

adjudication.rationale: In `AddGuestsDialog` the onError handler builds `const message = `${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}`;` and then calls `showToast(message || t("unable_to_add_guests"), ...)`. A template literal always returns a (typically non-empty) string (e.g., `"undefined: booking_not_found"`), so the `unable_to_add_guests` fallback is effectively unreachable. Also, the code passes `t(err.message)` directly; if `err.message` is not a known locale key, the raw string/key will be shown to users (potentially exposing non-localized/internal error text).

adjudication_records.issue_text: Blacklist and duplicate attendee checks are case-sensitive, allowing Block@Example.com to bypass the blacklist and User@x.com to create duplicate attendee rows and duplicate email sends

adjudication.rationale: In `addGuests.handler.ts`, blacklist and existing-attendee checks compare raw `guest` strings case-sensitively: `!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)` and `guest === attendee.email`. Although blacklist entries are lowercased (`map((email) => email.toLowerCase())`), incoming `guests` are not normalized, so `Block@Example.com` can bypass. Similarly, `User@x.com` vs `user@x.com` will not be detected as a duplicate attendee. Additionally, the server schema (`addGuests.schema.ts`) does not enforce uniqueness, so duplicate emails in the input array can result in duplicate `createMany` inserts and duplicate email sends.

adjudication_records.issue_text: No idempotency or in-flight guard: concurrent addGuests requests race on reading booking.attendees before createMany commits, allowing duplicate attendee rows; client double-click is also unguarded

adjudication.rationale: The handler derives `uniqueGuests` from a prior `prisma.booking.findFirst({ include: { attendees: true } })` snapshot and then inserts via `attendees.createMany` (in `addGuests.handler.ts`). There is no explicit idempotency key, transaction/locking, or upsert/skipDuplicates logic shown, so concurrent calls could attempt to insert the same emails based on a stale read. However, whether duplicates can actually be created depends on DB-level uniqueness constraints or `createMany` options not shown in the diff, so it’s not a verifiable defect from the diff alone. On the client, the Add button uses `loading={addGuestsMutation.isPending}` but there’s no explicit disable/one-shot guard shown, and whether `Button` prevents double-clicks while loading isn’t verifiable here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Schema lacks z.number().int().positive() on bookingId and a max length on guests array, allowing unbounded write/email amplification in a single unbounded Promise.all

adjudication.rationale: The newly added input schema `ZAddGuestsInputSchema` in `addGuests.schema.ts` uses `bookingId: z.number()` and `guests: z.array(z.string().email())` with no `.int().positive()` constraint on `bookingId` and no `.max(...)` limit on `guests`. In `addGuests.handler.ts`, `guests` drives `prisma.booking.update(... attendees.createMany ...)` and also drives email fan-out via `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)`, which builds an `emailsToSend` array and executes `await Promise.all(emailsToSend)` without any cap. This enables potentially unbounded DB writes and email sending in a single request (amplification/DoS risk), and the lack of integer/positive validation on `bookingId` is also a concrete schema weakness introduced by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: replyTo header in organizer-add-guests-email grows unboundedly with attendee count across repeated add-guests operations, potentially exceeding SMTP header limits and causing email rejection

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/emails/templates/organizer-add-guests-email.ts`, the `replyTo` header is constructed as `[this.calEvent.organizer.email, ...this.calEvent.attendees.map(({ email }) => email)]`, which includes *all* attendee emails on every “add guests” notification. Since the attendees list grows as guests are added (`addGuests.handler.ts` updates `booking.attendees` by creating more records), repeated add-guests operations will send organizer emails with an ever-larger Reply-To list. This can realistically exceed SMTP/header size limits for large attendee counts and cause delivery/rejection issues, which is broken behavior attributable to this diff.
